correctness.rationale: Every Boolean noun term is componentwise on disjoint unions, so each of the four atomic comparison forms is preserved, proving additive closure of any nonempty finite spectrum. Each nonempty additive subsemigroup of positive integers is generated by its least element and least members of occupied residue classes modulo that element. With h equal to the sum of positive generators, k=max(1,ceil(log2 h)) Boolean variables provide at least h disjoint atom terms. Empty unused atoms and pairwise equality of atom cardinalities within each generator block force precisely the positive nonnegative combinations of those generators; the converse partitions give all combinations. Contradictory sentences give the empty spectrum. The proof handles finite nonempty universes and infinite theories. The reproducible checker independently tested 206459 finite cell-count vectors and 409600 atomic disjoint-union implications. This bounded testing is supporting evidence rather than proof of an infinite statement.

value.rationale: Jiang 2026 Section 5.1 explicitly highlights the expressivity jump from allowing noun union and constructs only a single multiples-of-three spectrum. A natural next question is the complete family of possible finite spectra for exactly that language. The new necessity/sufficiency classification answers it for all (including infinite) theories, and produces a finite theory plus explicit raw-variable upper bound from any positive additive semigroup generators. It handles mixed generators and all infinite semigroups, not merely another divisibility or parity example, and demarcates the expressive power of noun-level versus sentence-level Boolean operations.
